title: Flooding: the long road from warning to recovery
label: 17 November 2026 · Flooding and emergency response
summary: The committee heard that floods can cause lasting emotional, health and financial harm, while help often becomes hard to find once emergency crews leave. Witnesses called for clearer warnings and recovery support, better coordination between public bodies and communities, and more reliable funding for flood protection, farming and emergency services. They also disagreed on whether new legal duties are needed, but shared concerns about gaps in accountability and resources.

chapters.title: Flooding’s lasting human cost
chapters.takeaway: Flood damage is not just physical: its effects on health, finances and peace of mind can last for years.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What does flooding do to people, businesses and communities?

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: The visible damage is only a small part of it. A flood can change people’s lives permanently, bringing trauma, anxiety and a long recovery. Communities often fill gaps in the official response, but that puts pressure on local people.

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: Families and businesses can face large costs before grants arrive, even if they’re insured. We hear that around two-thirds of people who’ve flooded have mental health problems, while only about half get any professional practical or wellbeing support.

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: Floods can damage soil for years and disrupt moving livestock, planting crops and managing farm finances. Farmers we surveyed said they’d spent about £40,000 on average responding to climate events over the past decade—a serious burden on businesses with very thin margins.

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: There’s an emotional cost for farmers and their families too. But farmers also want to help prevent floods and respond when they happen.

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: People tell us they can’t sleep when it rains, keep watch on water levels and no longer feel safe at home. Flooding can also mean time off work and costs that insurance doesn’t repay. In one community, people were still suffering breathing problems 12 years after homes weren’t properly dried.

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: A study of businesses in Shrewsbury found costs nearly 50% higher than the official figures. The effects can last one to three years, or for a lifetime. One study found that only 10% of people who sought mental health support managed to access it.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Does the mental strain mainly affect people in rural areas or those who’ve flooded repeatedly?

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: It can affect anyone who has flooded or come close. Even people who’ve spent a lot on protection can feel anxious whenever it rains.

chapters.title: Warnings and community readiness
chapters.takeaway: Warnings need to tell people what to do, while communities need support rather than being left to manage emergencies alone.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: How could communication before, during and after floods be improved?

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: Warnings matter, but they need accurate, local information about what people should do and where to get help. Some places face flood risk for the first time, so messages must be clear without causing unnecessary panic.

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: Local plans work best when farmers understand how their area behaves in both floods and droughts. We’ve seen good examples in Somerset and Lincolnshire, but elsewhere decisions still travel through informal WhatsApp groups and can arrive too late.

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: It varies too much from place to place. About one-third of people at risk in England don’t know they’re at risk. People also say warnings can be too early or too late, and they miss the local interpretation that once helped them judge what to do.

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: Communities can help monitor water and alert neighbours, but they need training, equipment and funding. We also need a single place to ask for help, including a phone service for people who can’t rely on online information.

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: A central contact point would help, but it shouldn’t replace local experts who know the area. We need both: one place to collect information and local people able to give practical advice.

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: A Government-led information point could be trusted and consistent, but it must connect to local councils that know the area and have the resources to act. People who’ve flooded may already be watching for danger; those who haven’t need help understanding their risk and what to do.

turns.speaker: Ben Goldsborough
turns.text: How much does it cost communities to prepare when lots of different public bodies are involved?

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: It takes time and money, and volunteers can feel isolated or under-equipped. Sometimes the people volunteering are dealing with flood damage at home themselves. Households and businesses also lose income; one report put the average household loss at £3,000.

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: Protecting a home can cost thousands, and many people can’t afford it. But preparation pays: one estimate says every pound spent beforehand saves eight pounds in future flood costs.

turns.speaker: Terry Jermy
turns.text: Do official emergency-planning groups work closely enough with local volunteers?

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: Not consistently. Some local resilience forums work well with communities; others feel distant and hard to approach, so residents simply organise among themselves.

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: Where communities have people willing and able to help, give them resources and training. But don’t assume every community has volunteers or can take on official responsibilities. Plans must account for people who are vulnerable or isolated.

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: Farmers are often the first to spot a breach, fallen cables or other danger, but can feel unable to act because of rules about land access, responsibility or insurance. They want to help, so local plans should give them clear permission and ways to contribute.

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: We rely too much on volunteers without supporting them enough. Some flood wardens have faced abuse for closing roads and need practical and emotional support.

chapters.title: Water management and farming
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses said flood plans must consider entire river areas, farmland and future water needs, not just homes in the immediate danger zone.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Farmers can be told to pump water away in winter, then find there’s not enough to use in summer. How can that be improved?

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: We need to store winter water for summer use, which means funding, planning permission and permission to fill reservoirs. The Government’s proposed water infrastructure grant could help; around 200 farmers are ready to build reservoirs if those pieces come together.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should farmers be paid when they hold floodwater on their land?

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: Yes. If farmers hold water back to protect communities downstream, they should be properly compensated.

turns.speaker: Charlie Dewhirst
turns.text: Are there good examples of agencies working together to manage rural flooding?

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: There aren’t enough. Internal drainage boards do important work, but they need to be fit for today’s needs and have the ability to manage water, not just pump it. Lincolnshire’s response plan has worked well and could offer lessons for other areas.

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: Plans should look across the whole river area and address different kinds of flooding. Water can build up in towns because drainage is already over capacity, so action upstream—including natural flood management and built drainage—can help.

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: Rural flooding matters too: it affects food production and can repeatedly isolate communities. For surface-water flooding, people often can’t tell if their home is at risk or which organisation to contact.

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: The Environment Agency should publish up-to-date information about the condition of its flood defences. Dry weather may have weakened them, but the latest figures we can see are months old, so communities can’t identify problems and act.

chapters.title: Recovery, grants and insurance
chapters.takeaway: People often face a long, confusing recovery after emergency crews leave, with uncertain grant rules and insurance that may not cover all needs.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: A resident described little communication after a major flood, with families still in temporary accommodation months later. Are people supported well enough once the emergency is over?

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: No. When emergency crews leave, it’s often unclear who takes charge. Recovery can last years and needs people who understand flooded households’ practical, emotional and financial needs.

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: Grant applications can involve a maze of paperwork. Councils may not have extra staff to process them, leaving people to pay for drying equipment or temporary housing while they wait. That’s especially hard for people without enough insurance.

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: Recovery means more than reopening roads. Farm losses can continue long after the immediate crisis, but farmers don’t know what rules the Government will use to decide whether help is available. Those rules should be clear in advance.

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: People often don’t know what help exists, if any. Even insured households can spend months or years arguing over repairs and managing contractors themselves while trying to recover and keep up with work and family life.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: Should there be clearer rules for when flood grants are activated?

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: Yes. The current decisions aren’t clear-cut and shouldn’t depend only on the number of homes affected. A flood that devastates a rural area may affect fewer properties than one in a town.

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: People who flood again may be unable to get some grants a second time, even though the damage and costs remain. Support should be available each time someone floods and needs it.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: Will people still be able to get flood insurance in the future?

turns.speaker: Tracey Garrett
turns.text: Flood Re currently helps many households, but it’s due to end in 2039. If the insurance market isn’t ready by then, thousands could struggle to get cover. Homes built after 2009 can’t use the scheme, including some new homes built in high-risk areas.

turns.speaker: Katia Sanhueza-Pino
turns.text: Without flood insurance, people may also struggle to get a mortgage. The ‘Build Back Better’ option can help pay for measures to make a home more flood-resilient, but it’s not available to everyone and the £10,000 limit is often below the average £30,000 cost of restoring a flooded home.

turns.speaker: Paul Tompkins
turns.text: Farmers in France can get help with flood insurance premiums when costs become unaffordable. Australia has a plan to help farmers invest in flood and drought resilience. We look at both examples with envy.

chapters.title: Who coordinates the response?
chapters.takeaway: Emergency crews often work effectively during the crisis, but unclear responsibilities and weak coordination can leave a gap when communities move into recovery.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: What makes it hard for public bodies to coordinate during a flood?

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: The immediate emergency response often works well, especially when agencies have practised together. The harder part is handing over from emergency response to the much longer recovery phase, when the work still needs people and resources.

turns.speaker: Councillor Matt Boughton
turns.text: Where local resilience forums have strong relationships, agencies usually work well together. But their effectiveness varies. They don’t have legal status, so decision-making, accountability and disagreements can become problems.

turns.speaker: Andrew McGill
turns.text: In the Wainfleet flood, drainage boards, the Environment Agency and fire crews worked well together. But after the immediate danger passed, local people were left with a huge job. Normal rules can also stop people acting quickly, even when the emergency is still unfolding.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: What would help the Environment Agency work better with drainage boards?

turns.speaker: Andrew McGill
turns.text: It needs to trust capable drainage boards to maintain more watercourses. The Environment Agency often focuses on the danger to homes, while drainage boards also manage water levels for the wider area, including farmland and other needs.

turns.speaker: Andrew McGill
turns.text: Some watercourses aren’t maintained because the agency lacks money, but it can still be difficult for another competent organisation to do the work. I’ve discussed simpler arrangements with the Government, but there’s been little progress so far.

turns.speaker: Councillor Matt Boughton
turns.text: In my area, we work well with the Environment Agency, including on flood warnings and protecting individual homes. But when it changes water levels at a flood-storage site, it can protect one area while increasing risk elsewhere. That’s why agencies need quick, clear communication and relationships built before a flood.

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: The fire service has no legal duty specifically to rescue people from floods. A clear legal responsibility would help us plan, prepare and understand how our role fits with the Environment Agency and councils.

turns.speaker: Helena Dollimore
turns.text: A flood linked to a water company’s failure cost the fire service £27,000 to respond. Can it recover those costs?

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: Not through a straightforward process, as far as I know. Fire crews responded to 17,000 flood incidents last year, and it’s difficult to recover the cost. I’d support a way to claim it back when a private company caused the flooding.

turns.speaker: Councillor Matt Boughton
turns.text: Councils should bring people together after floods, but utilities must also take responsibility when their failure caused the problem. The law should require them to work with councils and take part in planning, rather than leaving it to goodwill.

turns.speaker: Dr Roz Savage
turns.text: Should there be a required review after major floods, so agencies and communities can explain what went wrong and what should change?

turns.speaker: Andrew McGill
turns.text: Reviews can help. After Wainfleet, residents and agencies met again to discuss future protection. Keeping those conversations going matters because people can remain frightened long after a flood.

turns.speaker: Councillor Matt Boughton
turns.text: Councils would review incidents, but they’re already stretched and would need funding if that became a legal responsibility. The review also has to happen while they prepare for the next emergency.

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: Agencies often review their own work, but communities need a chance to speak too. Local resilience forums could bring everyone together after serious or repeated floods. Whether that must be a legal duty or encouraged good practice is open to debate.

chapters.title: Funding and responsibility
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses called for sustainable funding and clearer duties, while noting that changing the law alone won’t fix weak relationships or limited capacity.

turns.speaker: Ben Goldsborough
turns.text: Is the current funding system for drainage boards sustainable?

turns.speaker: Andrew McGill
turns.text: No. One board’s electricity bill rose from about £344,000 to more than £1 million in a year. Grants focus heavily on protecting homes, which can leave areas that support farming and food production at a disadvantage.

turns.speaker: Andrew McGill
turns.text: A grant application can take around 200 hours of staff time. The system needs to recognise the value of drainage to farming and the wider country, and make funding simpler to obtain.

turns.speaker: Councillor Matt Boughton
turns.text: Local councils’ payments to drainage boards have risen, but councils aren’t getting extra money to cover them. That means cuts elsewhere, so the current arrangement can’t continue indefinitely.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: Should utilities and other infrastructure companies have stronger duties to prepare for floods and join exercises?

turns.speaker: Councillor Matt Boughton
turns.text: Yes. Their legal responsibilities are lighter than those of emergency services and councils, even though damage to water, energy or transport systems can affect everyone. It can also be very difficult to get them to act on councils’ advice.

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: They should take part in exercises so agencies can test whether emergency plans work. We also need national coordination when several areas need the same limited fire-service resources at once.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The law dividing emergency organisations into category 1 and category 2 responders is more than 20 years old. Should it be reviewed?

turns.speaker: Phil Garrigan
turns.text: The categories help define who is responsible for what, but it’s sensible to check whether the law still works and whether organisations should be required to take part in exercises.

turns.speaker: Councillor Matt Boughton
turns.text: Yes, especially for category 2 organisations such as utilities, whose role in preparing for and responding to emergencies has become more important.

turns.speaker: Andrew McGill
turns.text: Drainage boards aren’t included in those categories, even though they work closely with the organisations that are.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: The central message is that flood response can work well at the height of an emergency, but people need clearer help and sustained support after the emergency crews leave.
